parts.problem_md:
A student investigates vitamin C in apple juice.

The student is provided with half an apple and some apple juice.

Fig. 1.1 shows the cut surface of the apple provided.

![Black and white close-up of a circular apple slice, showing smooth pale flesh and a central star-shaped seed pattern.](assets/001-black-and-white-close-up-of-a-circular-apple-sli.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

In the box, make a large drawing of the cut surface of the apple shown in Fig. 1.1.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Size: more than 50% of the box **[1 mark]**
> - Quality: continuous smooth outline with no shading **[1 mark]**
> - Detail: five core sections shown in a star-like shape with some pip halves **[1 mark]**
> 
> Ignore inner lines

> **[exam-tip]**
> Biological drawings should use single, clean continuous lines with no shading or sketchy double lines — practise drawing outlines slowly and deliberately rather than shading in detail.

parts.problem_md:
The student tests the apple juice using DCPIP.

DCPIP is a dark blue solution that turns colourless when vitamin C is added.

The greater the amount of vitamin C in the apple juice, the fewer the drops of apple juice needed to turn the DCPIP colourless.

**Procedure:**

The student:

- puts 2.0 cm<sup>3</sup> DCPIP into a test-tube
- fills a syringe with 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of apple juice
- adds apple juice to the DCPIP in the test-tube until the DCPIP turns colourless
- records in Table 1.1 the volume of apple juice remaining in the syringe for experiment 1.

The student repeats the procedure and records the volume of apple juice remaining in the syringe for experiment 2 in Table 1.1.

The student repeats the procedure again for experiment 3.

Fig. 1.2 shows the volume of apple juice remaining in the syringe in experiment 3.

![Diagram of an upright syringe marked in cubic centimetres, showing 1 cm³ of grey apple juice remaining at the bottom, labelled ‘apple juice remaining’.](assets/002-diagram-of-an-upright-syringe-marked-in-cubic-ce.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

(i) Record in Table 1.1 the volume of apple juice remaining in the syringe in experiment 3.

**Table 1.1**

| experiment | volume of apple juice remaining in syringe / cm³ | volume of apple juice added to the DCPIP / cm³ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.3 | 8.7 |
| 2 | 1.5 | 8.5 |
| 3 |   |   |

[1]

(ii) Calculate the volume of apple juice added to the DCPIP in experiment 3.

Record your answer in Table 1.1.

[1]

(iii) Calculate the average volume of apple juice added.

[1]

(iv) Suggest why the student repeats the experiment.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (i) 1.4 **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) 8.6 **[1 mark]**
> - (iii) 8.9 **[1 mark]**
> - (iv) To minimise the effect of random error by averaging / to identify any anomalous results **[1 mark]**
> 
> ecf from (b)(i); ecf from (b)(ii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question gives you a diagram of an instrument reading (like the syringe here), always read that value first — it feeds directly into every later calculation in the question, so an early misread costs multiple marks.

parts.problem_md:
You will test the apple juice using DCPIP.

DCPIP is a dark blue solution that turns colourless when vitamin C is added.

The greater the amount of vitamin C in the apple juice, the fewer the drops of apple juice needed to turn the DCPIP colourless.

(i) **Procedure**

- Use a pipette to put 4 drops of DCPIP into each of three test-tubes.
- Use a clean pipette to add drops of apple juice to one of the test-tubes until the solution becomes colourless. Count the number of drops as you add them.
- Record the number of drops added. This is experiment 1. Record your results in Table 1.1.
- Repeat with the other two test-tubes (experiment 2 and experiment 3) and record your results in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1 **

| Experiment | Number of drops of apple juice added |
|---|---|
| 1 |   |
| 2 |   |
| 3 |   |

(ii) Calculate the average number of drops of apple juice added for the three experiments.

[1]

(iii) Suggest one limitation of using a pipette in this procedure

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (i) All results recorded, with all three values within 10% of each other **[2 marks]**
> - (ii) Correct calculation of the average **[1 mark]**
> - (iii) Volume of drops not known accurately / may need half a drop to reach the endpoint / drops might be different sizes **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A pipette measures drops, not a fixed volume — the main limitation is always that drop size can vary slightly, which affects the precision of a "number of drops" measurement.

parts.problem_md:
The data shows the concentrations of sugar and starch in an onion.

| total sugar including reducing sugar (g per 100 g) | starch (g per 100 g) |
|---|---|
| 3.7 | 0.0 |

The onion is tested with Benedict's solution and iodine solution.

Which set of results is correct?

|   | Benedict’s solution | iodine solution |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | blue | blue-black |
| **B** | blue | yellow-brown |
| **C** | red | blue-black |
| **D** | red | yellow-brown |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Reducing sugar is present (3.7 g per 100 g), so Benedict's solution turns red
- No starch is present (0.0 g per 100 g), so iodine solution stays yellow-brown

**A** is incorrect because it shows a positive result for starch, but no starch is present

**B** is incorrect because it shows a negative result for reducing sugar, but reducing sugar is present

**C** is incorrect because it shows a positive result for starch, but no starch is present
